name: Tara Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does your workday usually look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and fit kitchen units and trim on building sites. I have a trade certificate and enough years behind me to do a sound job, though I am not the fastest fitter on the crew. I use AI every morning to check the parts list before the van goes out, then measure the actual wall. My partner and I have grown children and a few months of expenses saved; I hope to retire from regular site work at sixty-six in 2034 if the household figures allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the young fitters that the AI list saves a trip for a missing hinge, but nobody should skip the tape measure. An AI kitchen list cannot square a crooked building wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my normal wage to continue. A few months saved and some nearby fitting jobs give us room, though my partner and I still need to check whether retiring at sixty-six is affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting kitchens and showing apprentices how to mark a filler strip. I would use my existing daily AI list and review our expected age-sixty-six income against the household bills with my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work in this picture. The tool helps with parts, and the retirement calculation is something we needed anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you make an apprentice do before opening the parts list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Measure the wall and mark where it bows. A cabinet cut to a perfect drawing can leave a very visible gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would checking retirement costs mean you plan to leave now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I will stay on paid site work and decide closer to sixty-six, after we see income and bills in the same column.

say: I would **keep** measuring real walls while using AI for kitchen parts.
I would **teach** apprentices to mark a filler strip before cutting.
think: My **fitting** wage looks safe, but age-sixty-six retirement needs real income figures.
**Current** daily AI use is routine, not a new course or new skill.
do: **Keep** fitting kitchens and teaching apprentices to measure filler strips.
**Review** age-sixty-six retirement income against household bills with partner.
feel: **Calm** about present paid work and familiar AI use.
S0.quote: An AI kitchen list cannot square a crooked building wall.
fieldNote: **Tara** uses AI daily for parts while preserving physical kitchen measurements and apprenticeship habits.
She **has** typical pay, moderate savings and some local jobs; retirement remains an income question.

steps.text: Keep fitting site kitchens and teaching apprentices
Check age-sixty-six retirement figures before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say quicker buying could stop missing cabinet doors, and I would learn any new AI ordering controls early. I would still insist that a named fitter checks the installed cabinet before the builder signs off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A faster AI kitchen order is no bargain if the fitter loses a paid day to a tighter schedule. We have a few months saved, but losing a regular day each week would make the age-sixty-six retirement plan harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practice the new ordering controls on a completed kitchen and compare the delivery with the old list. I would keep fitting shifts and ask for written rates and paid hours if the builder changes targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about possible hours loss, though I can learn the tool and speak to the builder. I would rather compete by doing sound work than ask anyone to guarantee my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test on the completed kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether every hinge, panel and filler was counted and delivered before the fitters arrived. I would keep the old list beside the new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the builder about a shorter week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the hours on two kitchens and ask for the rate in writing. If the cut lasted, I would apply to a posted nearby fitter role only at household-covering pay.

say: I would **learn** new AI ordering controls and test them against real kitchen deliveries.
I would **insist** on a named person checking installed cabinets before sign-off.
think: **Tighter** schedules could cost a paid day and weaken retirement saving.
I **favour** useful tools and earned wages, but not an unmeasured target.
do: **Practice** new AI ordering controls on a completed building-site kitchen.
**Keep** paid fitting shifts while checking written hours and rates.
**Apply** after sustained cuts to posted local fitter job at household-covering wage.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible paid-hour cuts before retirement.
S1.quote: A faster AI kitchen order is no bargain if the fitter loses a paid day to a tighter schedule.
fieldNote: Her **adaptability** means actual practice with new controls, not merely viewing an existing output.
Her **traditional** work ethic coexists with concern that management may cut her own paid hours.

steps.text: Learn new AI ordering controls on actual kitchen records
Keep paid fitting shifts while checking hours
Apply after cuts to posted local fitter role at adequate wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI comes in 2028 when I am sixty, and capable hands-on robots around 2031 when I am sixty-three. A kitchen robot in 2031 could take three paid years before my planned retirement at sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a builder could cut my paid kitchen shifts once robots fit standard units. A few months saved will not fund three years, and I do not want our grown children to make up the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid fitting work and ask for a supervised, paid trial checking robot-fitted cabinets for safe wall fixings. If my hours fall, I would apply to posted nearby repair-fitting jobs only if the wage covers our bills and the site lets a person stop unsafe work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about those three possible lost years, but I can test a role and search locally. I would not call retiring at sixty-three a plan unless verified income covered the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with a robot-fitted cabinet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loose wall fixing can let a loaded cupboard fall. I would require an exposed fixing check before anyone signs the kitchen over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain immediately for checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a course is fully funded, its training days are paid and a suitable posted local role offers enough pay. I would not enroll on an advertisement alone.

say: **Thinking** AI changes ordering in 2028; robot fitting threatens paid kitchen work around 2031.
I would **require** a paid supervised safety trial before signing robot work.
think: **Three** wage years before my target cannot be replaced by a few months saved.
A **real** local repair job needs bill-covering pay and stop-work authority.
do: **Keep** paid kitchen shifts while seeking supervised paid robot-checking trial.
**Apply** after hours fall to posted local repair role with adequate pay and safety authority.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost fitting years, with local alternatives.
S2.quote: A kitchen robot in 2031 could take three paid years before my planned retirement at sixty-six.
fieldNote: Her **proposal** checks cabinet fixings and gives a human authority to stop unsafe work.
**Course** interest remains only an enquiry; she would require funding, paid days and a posted adequate local job before enrolling.

steps.text: Keep paid kitchen shifts during supervised paid robot-checking trial
Apply after cuts to posted local repair job with adequate pay and stop-work authority
Enrol in fully funded paid-time course only for posted local role at bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am sixty-three, and capable site robots around 2034 when I am sixty-six. If our original retirement target is affordable, the physical robots arrive as I leave regular kitchen fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still want work that pays until that age, and the budget might tell us to continue. I could train as an installation checker if a funded course on paid days, a posted local vacancy and a proper salary all line up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting kitchens and check the age-sixty-six income with my partner. If a local checker role is posted at a wage covering our bills, with safety sign-off authority and a fully funded paid-time course, I would enroll and apply after qualifying; if our retirement figures work, I would leave at the original target instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy until the figures are clear. Five years lets me check the course and the retirement plan rather than promise either one today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a checker role genuine to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written vacancy naming the site, the pay and the authority to stop a poor cabinet fixing. A kitchen inspection certificate cannot hold a cupboard up unless the paid checker can stop a bad fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is leaving at sixty-six an early retirement response?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It is the age I already had in mind. We would do it only if the household income actually covered the bills.

say: **Robots** in 2034 arrive at my existing age-sixty-six retirement target.
I would **take** formal checking training only with paid time, funding and a real local role.
think: The **household** budget decides whether I retire or need more paid kitchen work.
A **checker** must have written safety authority and a wage covering our bills.
do: **Enroll** in funded paid-time checking course for posted adequate local safety role if work continues.
**Apply** after qualification to posted local checker job with adequate pay and stop-work authority.
feel: **Uneasy** while household income and job terms remain uncertain.
S3.quote: A kitchen inspection certificate cannot hold a cupboard up unless the paid checker can stop a bad fixing.
fieldNote: She **keeps** 2034 robot work conditional on whether her pre-existing retirement target is affordable.
**Actual** training and application require funding, paid time, a posted local job, adequate wage and safety authority.

steps.text: Check existing age-sixty-six retirement budget before deciding
Enrol if retirement unaffordable in funded paid-time course for posted bill-covering local safety role
Apply after qualifying if income short to posted local checker with bill-covering pay and stop authority
Retire at original 2034 target instead if household income covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am sixty-eight and capable robots around 2039 when I am seventy-one. Both dates are after my hoped-for retirement at sixty-six in 2034, if the budget supports it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot fitting kitchens in 2039 cannot replace a wage I stopped needing in 2034, if our sums hold. If the figures do not work, I may still be fitting or checking kitchens in 2036 and would need an actual local vacancy, not a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep current paid fitting shifts and check the age-sixty-six income with my partner. If it covers our bills, I would retire at the original 2034 target; if not, I would keep working and apply only to posted nearby kitchen-checking roles with adequate pay and authority to stop unsafe work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the household calculation but calm about the distant robot date if we can stop as planned. Ten years is time to verify, not a promise that I will work at seventy-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep using AI after leaving site work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps for household lists, but that is not a job plan. I would first want the income figures to cover ordinary expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you cannot retire at sixty-six?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep earning in fitting or a posted safe local checker role at a wage that covers the bills. I would not ask our grown children to subsidise an early exit.

say: My **planned** 2034 exit comes before 2036 thinking AI and 2039 robots if affordable.
I would **keep** earning if verified retirement income falls short.
think: A **posted** local checker role with adequate pay and safety authority would matter only if I still work.
**Daily** AI use today does not imply a job at seventy-one.
do: **Keep** current paid kitchen fitting while verifying retirement costs.
**Retire** at original 2034 target only if income covers ongoing bills.
**Apply** if still working to posted local checker role with adequate pay and safety authority.
feel: **Uneasy** until retirement figures are checked, otherwise calm about distant robots.
S4.quote: A robot fitting kitchens in 2039 cannot replace a wage I stopped needing in 2034, if our sums hold.
fieldNote: Her **continued** site work after 2034 is explicitly conditional on retirement income being insufficient.
The **original** age-sixty-six exit is not early retirement; any later application requires real safe local work and adequate pay.

steps.text: Keep paid fitting until retirement income is verified
Retire at original 2034 target only if household income covers bills
Apply if still working to posted local safe checker role with adequate pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast case worries me most because 2031 robots could cut kitchen-fitting shifts three years before I hoped to retire. A paid safety trial and a posted local repair role at household-covering wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a checker has the right to stop an unsafe cabinet fixing. I will use a clever tool, but somebody must be allowed to say the cupboard is not ready. My trade certificate taught me to fix a cabinet; my retirement budget decides when I can stop fixing them.

headlineQuote: My trade certificate taught me to fix a cabinet; my retirement budget decides when I can stop fixing them.
portrait: **Tara** is a fifty-eight-year-old trade-certified kitchen fitter with a partner and grown children.
She **earns** typical pay, has one to six months saved and some local construction jobs.
She **uses** AI every day, learns new controls early and values apprenticeships and earned work.
She **hopes** to retire at sixty-six in 2034 if income covers bills; later site work remains conditional.
biggestWorry: **Fast** robots around 2031 could cut paid kitchen work three years before her hoped-for age-sixty-six exit.
whatWouldHelp: A **supervised** paid safety trial and a posted local repair job at household-covering wages would help.
